item.title: Proxmox ships with settings that waste power and disk space, and one cleanup fixes both
item.itunes:title: Proxmox ships with settings that waste power and disk space, and one cleanup fixes both
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Proxmox is a hypervisor built for always-on servers that never get a break from duty, and because of that, the defaults set when you install it on your home lab aren't necessarily the most optimal. On a fresh install it can hold your CPU at higher clocks than necessary and waste disk space on the SSD you boot from. For a home server or lab that idles the vast majority of the time that it's on, these small defaults can add up, but thankfully, saner settings are relatively easy to configure.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover
I tried moving my home lab off Proxmox multiple times, but nothing came close to replacing it

Proxmox is in a league of its own when it comes to home lab projects

3
By  Ayush Pande

Proxmox will run your CPU like it's always under load

It'll keep the clocks higher than they need to be set

Potentially the biggest waste of power on your Proxmox box is the CPU. By default, the CPU governor is set to the performance mode, which isn't a problem on the surface, but for a home box that's not doing much 99% of the time, it's a big waste. The CPU governor is the Linux kernel setting that decides how high your CPU clocks itself, and setting it to performance tells it to stay near its maximum frequency regardless of the load. To see what yours is set at, you can use the command: cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cpufreq/scaling_governors.

What you switch to depends on what CPU you have and which driver is active. Most modern AMD and Intel chips one would have in a Proxmox box would be running intel_pstate or amd-pstate-epp and only offer performance and powersave options. In the powersave mode, your clocks will still ramp up under load, but if your driver is listed as acpi-cpufreq, powersave will lock the CPU at its lowest frequency regardless of load, which isn't what you want either. schedutil is what you would want instead in that case. Check which driver you have with the command: cat /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu0/cpufreq/scaling_driver before making any changes.

There's no GUI toggle for this, but there is a community script available called PVE CPU Scaling Governor that shows your current governor and switches it, along with adding a cron entry so it's not wiped with a reboot. To do it manually, you can take a governor for a spin first before making it permanent with the command echo powersave | tee /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpu*/cpufreq/scaling_governor, where powersave is the governor of choice.

To make it permanent, you add cpufreq.default_governor=powersave to GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT in /etc/default/grub and run update-grub. Hosts that boot with systemd-boot will need the same parameter put in /etc/kernel/cmdline, followed by proxmox-boot-tool refresh. Some guest operating systems can cope poorly with frequency changes, so if you find your VMs acting up after the change, I'd swap it back as a troubleshooting measure first.

I built a home lab on a PC that was headed to the recycling bin, and Proxmox made it free to run

The perfect way to reuse an old PC

By  Ty Sherback

ASPM is what allows for deeper idle

Another small tweak that can make a difference

Editing the CPU governor only covers the cores and their clock speeds, but it doesn't cover the other devices in your system. Part of getting the rest of your system into deeper idle states is PCIe Active State Power Management (ASPM).

ASPM can be checked with lspci -vv | grep ASPM, and you'll be looking for mentions of LnkCtl: ASPM Enabled. LnkCap: will show what the link supports, so if you see anything like ASPM not supported, that means the device cannot be configured with ASPM. Toggling ASPM is done through the BIOS, so after you turn it on and reboot, rerun the command to check if it took effect.

One caveat: Intel’s I225 and I226 2.5GbE controllers—exceedingly common in mini PCs home labbers use—have a documented habit of dropping off the network when ASPM is enabled, so make sure you can reach the host’s console before you flip it on.

4 Proxmox changes I made that delivered 90% of my reliability gains

These Proxmox tricks made my self-hosting and experimentation server more reliable

By  Ayush Pande

Storage thinning

Proxmox's defaults here don't make sense for a home user

Every VM you create in Proxmox by default has the "Discard" setting unchecked. The Discard setting controls whether the hypervisor tells the bare metal storage if certain blocks are free or not, and it ends up having a pretty big impact on your system's storage.

When a guest deletes a file, its filesystem doesn't really erase that thing, it just marks those blocks as free in its own records. This is where TRIM comes in: the guest will later send a list of blocks it no longer needs, either on a schedule through fstrim, or immediately if Discard is checked in the Proxmox GUI.

With Discard off, QEMU drops the guest's TRIM requests. The guest doesn't know any better, and it thinks it trimmed properly. With it on, QEMU turns each request into a real deallocation operation on the backing storage. Without Discard enabled, a thin-provisioned disk only ever grows.

This is a problem in terms of capacity, but it also affects drive endurance. On a default install, the LVM thin pool passes discards through to the physical drive. You can confirm this with lvs -o+discards pve/data, which should report passdown. A TRIM that leaves the guest can then travel all the way to the SSD’s controller, which marks those flash pages invalid.

An SSD can’t overwrite data in place, though: before it erases a block, it has to copy every page it still thinks is live somewhere else. When it knows which pages are dead, garbage collection has less work to do in copying, and that means fewer internal writes, saving some drive health in the process. With Discard off, that information stops at the hypervisor, and the drive keeps carefully preserving data the guest deleted months ago.

The potential downside of enabling Discard can come in the form of high performance overhead when performing live migrations, which isn't something you'll often be doing as a home lab user. You can comfortably enable it on your VMs.

I always tweak my Proxmox host's settings before spinning up a single VM or LXC

It's the only way I set up a Proxmox node now

1
By  Ayush Pande

Proxmox defaults are for the enterprise, not the home user

They're an excellent fit for large clusters that are in charge of a large number of users, but Proxmox's defaults are often made without considering the home user at all. One short session of tweaking can bring your home lab more in line with how you actually want it to run, which should be cool, quiet, and not hammering the solid-state storage that is only getting more expensive.

item.title: This open-source browser has quietly replaced the most used app on my desktop
item.itunes:title: This open-source browser has quietly replaced the most used app on my desktop
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I never expected a web browser to replace Adobe Acrobat, one of the most frequently used applications on my desktop. For years, opening, reviewing, and editing PDFs meant launching Acrobat, even for minor changes. That changed when I started exploring Mozilla Firefox beyond its browsing capabilities. Its built-in PDF tools turned out to be far more capable than I expected, handling most of the tasks that previously sent me straight to Acrobat. Before long, Firefox quietly became my go-to PDF application.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Firefox opens PDFs without making me launch another application

It makes opening and navigating PDFs feel effortless

One reason Firefox has become my default PDF viewer is its built-in PDF.js engine, Mozilla's open-source JavaScript-based PDF rendering technology. Once I set Firefox as the default PDF app in Windows, opening a document is as simple as double-clicking it in File Explorer. Windows launches the file in a Firefox tab rather than sending me to a separate reader. PDFs opened from links or the Downloads panel also appear in the browser, so there's no need to save every file before viewing it.

Firefox's PDF viewer doesn't feel stripped down, either. It offers familiar controls for page navigation, zooming, and jumping to a specific page. A sidebar displays page thumbnails, making it easier to scan lengthy documents. Firefox also supports document outlines when the PDF includes them, along with a search box for locating specific words or phrases. Switching between open PDFs and regular websites using tabs keeps research and reference material together, and it makes the entire workflow feel more connected.

Organizing PDF pages doesn't require a new tool

Rearranging, merging, and extracting pages is surprisingly easy

The page sidebar proves particularly useful when working with lengthy PDFs. Instead of scrolling through the entire document, its thumbnail view lets me jump between pages and manage their order directly. Rearranging pages is as simple as dragging them into a new position. Multiple pages can be selected, copied, and pasted elsewhere, while unnecessary ones can be removed. The Undo option helps reverse changes that don't go as planned.

Combining documents is equally straightforward. Clicking the plus button in the sidebar lets me import another PDF and merge its pages with the document already open. This is a convenient way to bring related reports, receipts, or reference material into one file. I can export selected pages as a separate PDF, leaving the original file untouched. This saves me from sharing an entire report when someone only needs a specific section. The extracted pages are saved as a separate PDF, leaving the original file available for future reference.

I found a free Adobe Acrobat alternative that doesn’t compromise on features

A private, capable replacement for Acrobat

2
By  Parth Shah

The TCL NXTPAPER 11 Plus is an 11.45-inch Wi-Fi Android 15 tablet with an anti-glare NXTPAPER 4.0 display. It has a 2.2K 120Hz screen, a MediaTek Helio G100 processor with 8GB of RAM and 256GB of storage, an 8000mAh battery, and 33W charging.

The battery capacity is 8000 mAh, and the tablet supports 33W charging. The charger isn't included, so you'll have to use your own USB-C cable and charger.

That's 38% off TCL's regular price, and it's an easy one to pick up if you mostly read, take notes, and browse. Just be sure to grab the TCL NXTPAPER 11 Plus before the promotion ends on November 30.

item.title: I gave an old Android phone a second life as a Spotify Connect stereo, and it cost nothing
item.itunes:title: I gave an old Android phone a second life as a Spotify Connect stereo, and it cost nothing
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I listen to a lot of music in the kitchen while cooking or wrapping up chores. However, getting music into the space isn't easy. My old Google Nest Mini is a bit too small for the kind of music fidelity I want, while devices like the Echo Show are too unwieldy for simple stereo playback. Plus, there's the cost. I don't want to spend hundreds of dollars on a kitchen setup when I have a perfectly serviceable pair of bookshelf speakers lying around.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

So, I put on my DIY hat and decided to dig around for ways to turn one of my spare phones and bookshelf speakers into a Spotify Connect experience. That's where LibreThing comes in. This open-source Android project turns any old Android phone into a dedicated Spotify Connect receiver.

Instead of relying on Bluetooth pairing or keeping Spotify open on a phone, it creates a standalone music endpoint that appears within the Spotify Connect device picker. It lets me start playback from any device and keep the music playing completely hands-free.

Why LibreThing is better than leaving Spotify running on an old phone

Build a dedicated Spotify Connect receiver for free

My first instinct when building this project was to keep the Spotify app open and pinned with local discovery switched on. That's a reasonable approach. But that's not how the Spotify app is meant to be used, and it can be a bit unreliable when trying to connect to it. The interesting thing about LibreThing is that it implements the Spotify Connect protocol directly on the Android device so that it can act like any other streamer or connected speaker with Spotify Connect built in.

The project builds on top of go-librespot, which is a popular open-source implementation of Spotify Connect. LibreThing takes the engine and packages it into a native Android application with its own interface, settings, and background service, so you get a single APK to install instead of building the implementation through Termux.

You don't need a particularly powerful phone either. In fact, anything running Android 7 and above should work just fine, which means even a five-year-old phone sitting in your junk drawer should suffice. All you'll need is a network connection and a way to connect the device to your speakers. If your old phone supports a headphone jack, you're good to go. If not, a USB adapter dongle is your best friend.

LibreThing gives you a lot of options to configure your streaming experience

Set up Spotify Connect in minutes

Getting started is easier than you'd imagine. Just install the app using the APK provided on GitHub, and you're good to go. The app offers plenty of settings, but if your goal is just to get music going, hit install, tap the start button, and it'll immediately show up as a Spotify Connect device on your phone or laptop.

On the same Wi-Fi network, select the device as your Spotify Connect endpoint, and you'll see the album cover, track info, and a progress bar pop up on your phone. No sign-in needed. Since this runs on Spotify Connect, you can hand the music off from the kitchen speaker to any other speaker at home, and it'll continue playing from there. Music is great, but if you use Spotify for podcasts or audiobooks while working, you'll find this incredibly useful. And yes, since LibreThing is trying to recreate the experience of Spotify's short-lived Car Thing, you can even control playback from your smartphone's display.

As I mentioned, the app has plenty of built-in controls to customize your experience. For example, you'll find an option to activate a fake sleep feature. It turns the display completely black without stopping playback, which is pretty useful if you want to leave the phone playing for long periods. Often, I'll have a long playlist running while I'm getting things done. Having a sleep screen helps protect the old OLED screen.

In fact, there are additional OLED protections built in, like the ability to periodically shift interface elements, as well as a scheduled grayscale or red-light-only mode. I don't really need these for a kitchen speaker, but you might find them handy in the bedroom.

Among all the other settings available, there's one that particularly caught my eye. It's the ability to set a fixed playback quality level. I'm not particularly bandwidth-constrained, and I've got a decent set of bookshelf speakers installed in the kitchen, so I wanted the best possible audio quality. While you can't set it to lossless in LibreThing, 320 kbps is more than good enough for the purpose, and that's what I've set it to.

Give your old Android phone a second life

While my initial plan to use the Spotify app with some speakers plugged in would've worked well enough in short bursts, LibreThing has let me build a more bespoke setup without buying another piece of hardware.

I already have a set of speakers and more old Android phones than I know what to do with. Installing a single open-source app lets me build my own Spotify streaming setup that works just as well as a commercial streamer with little to no configuration. This one's an easy weekend project if you've been looking to add music around your home.

item.itunes:title: 4 Google apps I swapped for lightweight alternatives, and my Pixel feels faster
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Google apps are deeply woven into the Pixel experience, and it's easy to accept them as the default choices. But are they always the best options? I decided to try a different set of apps and see what I was missing. I wasn't looking for complicated replacements or tools with endless customization options. I wanted lightweight apps that handled their core jobs well and didn't demand more resources than necessary. The results made me rethink a few of my default choices.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Google Photos

Fossify Gallery keeps my photo library simple

Google Photos is convenient, but it always feels like more than just a gallery app. Between cloud features, automatic backups, AI-powered tools, and recommendations, there's quite a lot happening behind the scenes. For simply browsing pictures stored on the phone, that feels unnecessary. After trying a few alternatives, Fossify Gallery caught my attention because it keeps things focused on local photos. It focuses entirely on the photos already stored on the device, with a clean interface that doesn't get in the way of everyday use.

Even with a large photo collection, finding locally stored pictures felt more direct, without having to navigate through cloud libraries and additional recommendations. I also found its album organization easy to follow, making it convenient to jump between different folders and find specific pictures. Fossify Gallery includes useful options such as image editing, app locking, hidden albums, and a recycle bin. I didn't have to sign in or spend time setting up cloud backups just to browse my photos.

For someone who primarily uses their Pixel to capture and browse photos rather than manage an entire cloud library, Fossify Gallery makes a refreshing replacement.

Fossify Gallery

Fossify Gallery is a free, open-source, and ad-free photo and video gallery app for Android focused on privacy and local media management.

See at F-Droid

Gboard

HeliBoard gives me everything I need for typing

Replacing Gboard was a slightly different experiment because the keyboard is something I use throughout the day. I didn't want an alternative that sacrificed typing comfort just to offer a simpler interface. Gboard has plenty of smart features, including voice typing, translation, GIF search, and predictive suggestions, but most of my regular typing doesn't depend on them. HeliBoard offered a way to keep the essentials without carrying all those additional features.

The transition was easier than expected. HeliBoard supports multiple languages, custom themes, and a personal dictionary, so the basic typing experience didn't feel like a downgrade. Word suggestions and autocorrect were also useful enough for regular conversations and quick notes. HeliBoard was a practical switch, especially for someone who values a focused typing experience over a long list of additional tools.

By  Yash Patel

Google Maps

Organic Maps makes offline navigation easy

Google Maps is my go-to app for getting directions, but I don't always need everything it offers. When I'm simply trying to reach a destination, business recommendations, reviews, and other discovery features can be more than I need. That's where Organic Maps caught my attention. It focuses on navigation and offers offline maps, making it useful when I don't want to depend on a mobile data connection.

Built on OpenStreetMap data, the app provides detailed maps with driving, walking, and cycling navigation. Its offline capabilities quickly became one of its most useful features. I could download a city map before heading out and continue finding routes even in areas with unreliable mobile coverage. This also means less reliance on mobile data and fewer network requests. The app includes useful details such as hiking trails, points of interest, and public facilities.

The trade-off is that it doesn't offer Google's live traffic updates, extensive business reviews, or equally comprehensive local listings. For offline trips and straightforward route planning, Organic Maps has become a useful alternative, even if Google Maps remains more convenient for discovering businesses and checking live traffic.

Organic Maps

Organic Maps is a free, open-source offline navigation app for Android and iPhone, offering privacy-focused, ad-free maps, hiking trails, driving directions, bookmarks, and maps without tracking users or collecting data.

See at Organic Maps

Chrome

Brave makes web browsing less cluttered

Chrome works well for everyday browsing, but I wanted a browser that offered better privacy controls and didn't require me to install several extensions to customize my browsing experience. That's what led me to try Brave. It is based on Chromium, just like Chrome, so the browsing experience feels familiar. However, it comes with several privacy-focused tools built in, making it a more appealing option for people who want greater control over their web activity.

Brave Shields was one of the first features I noticed during testing. It blocks many ads and trackers automatically, making websites with aggressive advertising easier to browse. Blocking these unwanted elements can also reduce unnecessary network requests and the amount of content a webpage needs to load. I also liked being able to control how Brave handles cookies, trackers, and other unwanted content. Overall, Brave felt like a more comfortable browsing option, with useful privacy features already built in.

item.title: I replaced my homelab notes with a self-hosted Wiki.js 3.0 instance, and the long-awaited rewrite was worth the wait
item.itunes:title: I replaced my homelab notes with a self-hosted Wiki.js 3.0 instance, and the long-awaited rewrite was worth the wait
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I had been an active contributor to Wikipedia long before I jumped into technical writing and blogging. After school every day, I used to dive into Wikipedia articles and suggest edits wherever needed. But that was almost a decade ago. Today, the situation is totally different. I now host my own knowledge management app, Trilium.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

It contains details and information about my homelab. A few weeks ago, I was casually scrolling Reddit and came across a thread announcing that Wiki.js 3.x is out of beta after four years. I had no problems with Trilium, but my tinkerer mind couldn’t stop trying it because I was curious why it took four years, plus my history with Wikipedia.

My homelab notes were a mess

Trilium fixed it, until Wiki.js 3.0 landed

Years with my homelab taught me that scattered notes across different note apps are no use when I actually need them. And notes are very important when managing a homelab of 30+ containers across six different machines, a few VPSs, and networking gear.

Before Trilium, the homelab information was a mess. I had everything but not in one place, maybe a recovery code in my Apple Notes app, API keys in my PC’s document folder, or network config in an LLM chat. So during an actual emergency, I could never find them.

Trilium was proving to be a good fit for my workflow, and I had almost all the information about my homelab in just a few clicks. But after reading Wiki.js’s 3.0 release post, I started to think otherwise. It was a flashback to my Wikipedia editing days: the page history, diffs, and edit summaries.

According to the post, 3.0 was a complete rewrite after almost four years of development, and the highlights were the Markdown editor, file manager, content blocks, and a better timeline than Trilium’s.

After reading the full release post, I quickly jumped into deploying it in my homelab. I was already thinking it might replace Trilium for good. But the initial deployment was the easy step; moving my notes to it was another story.

I use Obsidian to document my home lab and self-hosted services, here's how

There are tools built for documenting your home lab, but I love using Obsidian for it instead.

5
By  Adam Conway

The import said success

I still couldn’t see a single page

Once it was deployed, I assumed I would export my notes from Trilium in one click and import them into Wiki.js in another. Well, only half of that was true in my case: the first part. I headed to Trilium to export my notes. It offered different export formats, but I chose Markdown because MD files were one of the highlights from the release I liked so much.

Because of my computer science background, I have a long relationship with MD files. But Trilium’s recommended export format was HTML, as it could keep all notes' formatting as is. I still went with Markdown even though Trilium warned me about it: “Preserves most formatting.” My notes were only text and a few tables, so it didn’t cost me much, though.

The export was saved to my local folder as a zip, with the same tree structure as in my notes. A main notes folder and a JSON file for metadata. Then I moved to the Wiki.js part. It wasn’t the one-click export I expected. It could only sync content with a folder on disk or a Git repo, and pages stay plain Markdown. I went with Local File System storage, but there were a few more options available, such as Google Cloud and Azure.

I unarchived the export zip and pointed Local File System storage at that folder. After that, I chose the option that fit in this situation: “Import Everything.” It successfully imported all the pages, but I couldn’t see them anywhere.

I put all of Wikipedia on my home server, and it still answers when the internet is down

We have Wikipedia at home

6
By  João Carrasqueira

Getting it running

It’s easy, with two catches

I’ll get to the missing pages, but first the installation hiccups. I copy-pasted the Docker Compose file from Wiki.js’ documentation and deployed it. I opened the local IP with the assigned port, and it went straight to the login page instead of the setup wizard I was expecting.

There was no sign-up option either. So, I went back to the documentation and found out that the default admin account comes from ADMIN_EMAIL and ADMIN_PASS variables, and since I booted without them, it created a placeholder admin. I thought adding both and redeploying would solve it, but it did nothing. I had to wipe the database and redeploy it again to get started.

Now, coming back to the major issue I faced after importing the notes. Even though the admin dashboard mentioned I had 18 pages, navigating to them was throwing a 404, saying the page didn’t exist.

After a few back-and-forth troubleshooting steps, I figured out that Trilium also used a tree structure in the URL. The root folder first, followed by the subfolders, for example, /Homelab/network, but Wiki.js read the top folder as the locale. So, I replaced the root folder name with the locale, for me "en," and it worked. The same issue was with the sidebar as well; it required a similar fix.

Trilium is on its way out

I haven't explored all the features Wiki.js offers yet, but even at this early glance, I am sure I am going to replace Trilium with it. Trilium, no doubt, is a good place to start, and it offers a few impressive features like LLM integration, but a personally familiar workflow is better than exciting features. Overall, if you're getting into homelabbing or are an old user without a centralized hub of information, Trilium or Wiki.js are probably the best places to start.

Wiki.js

Wiki.js is a free, open-source wiki you can self-host, with Markdown pages, built-in page history and folder or Git sync.

item.title: I gave my 9-year-old laptop server a local LLM job every night, and it reads my homelab logs so I don’t have to
item.itunes:title: I gave my 9-year-old laptop server a local LLM job every night, and it reads my homelab logs so I don’t have to
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
The most tedious task for an early homelabber is the logs. We have piles of logs for each service we host. We almost never open and read them since we rely on the monitoring services. Services like Beszel and Uptime Kuma do important work, but they are limited to specific jobs, and none of them read the actual logs.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

With LLMs these days, I usually hand over busy work to locally hosted models on my powerful workstation. But in the case of service logs from my server, it is not straightforward, because I can’t keep my workstation on all the time. So I pivoted and hosted a local LLM on my 9-year-old laptop server. It now runs every day at six in the morning and reports the findings to me.

A 2016 laptop handled it without a GPU

The first attempt wouldn’t stop thinking out loud

Why am I mentioning a 2016 laptop multiple times? Most people use repurposed or refurbished hardware as their first home server. And for me it was (it still is) a 9-year-old Dell Latitude laptop. The laptop was headed for recycling when my relative got a new laptop. So, instead of recycling it, I took the opportunity to repurpose it as my first home server, currently running more than 30 containers.

For context, the Latitude has an i5-6300U processor and 8 GB of memory. I added another 4 GB to it. So, an almost decade-old laptop with a mediocre CPU and no dedicated GPU. Even when thinking about it, I was unsure about my decision to host a local LLM on it. Nevertheless, I deployed Gemma 4 E2B Q4_K_M on llama.cpp.

I am not discussing why llama.cpp or why Gemma 4; I already covered that in my previous articles. Based on my previous experience, I simply configured the LLM the way I liked, and that suited this hardware. Context 8192, 2 threads and 2 CPUs, temperature 0.2, 1,200 max tokens, and reasoning off.

Gemma 4 E2B Q4_K_M is around 3GB; that means it could take up to 3GB of memory on load and more while running, so keeping it running all the time wasn’t practical. So, instead, I made it start the container, run, and remove it after the report. This way, the container won’t take unnecessary memory the whole day.

The first run was a bummer, though. Initially, I decided to go with the :light image running llama-cli. But when I ran the model, it started with the interactive prompt, which spent my token budget and generated a different output than I expected.

Even though the stats were decent, around 42 tokens per second for prompt processing and 10 for generation under two minutes, I still decided to switch to llama-server.

I gave a local LLM full control over my Proxmox node, and it worked better than I expected

It's actually good enough for simple management tasks

9
By  Ayush Pande

It caught what I’d have missed

It also called every error an upstream failure

The script was set to run every morning at 6 AM. Before even running it for the first time, I was casually scrolling through Portainer and noticed that my AdGuard Home (AGH) container was unhealthy. I knew exactly why it was unhealthy. I won’t go into details, but it was because of unassigned ports after a reboot and NetBird DNS taking over it.

I thought it was the best way to test the script and the LLM, so I kept the unhealthy status as is. In the first run (with llama-cli), it did tell me that my AdGuard container logged multiple failed upstream queries in 24 hours. Then I fixed the issue and ran the script again. This time the error was gone, and a new error appeared.

After that, I kept the script running for the next few days and checked the reports each day. It correctly flagged errors like a leftover wikijs_wikinet network, which then disappeared in the next digest, but it also flagged a few recurring errors that weren't important.

For example, after the AGH container status issue, it gave me a new harmless AGH error every day. Some were correct, and some were imprecise. In one report, 18 of the 20 AdGuard error lines were TLS errors, and only two were failed upstream queries, but still the model described all of them as “when querying external DNS servers.”

The recurring errors weren't the model’s fault, but it was configured in such a way that the model didn’t know what happened yesterday. So every day, the report was new for the model; hence; it acted that way.

I built a local LLM server I can access from anywhere, and it uses a Raspberry Pi

It may not replace ChatGPT, but it's good enough for edge projects

3
By  Ayush Pande

The model wasn’t the clever part

It only sees what my script lets through

You might be wondering how a small model like E2B was handling the logs from more than 30 containers. Processing that many logs in just two minutes looks very difficult. Yes, you are thinking in the right direction. I thought the same, which is why I decided to add a lot of filters to the script. So the reports were already filtered even before reaching the model.

The first was that it reads only the last 24 hours of logs from every running container, and only the lines matching error keywords like error, fail, denied, or timeout. After that, I added another filter to skip the ignore list so it wouldn't catch the one I was experimenting on. Then, it kept only the ranked and counted error list the script sorted because a day of logs may contain repeated lines. Even after the ranking, the logs were capped at 12,000 characters overall.

I also masked the numbers to differ lines only by a port or ID. These were the only ways to make an under-two-minute local LLM run on an old laptop with no dedicated GPU. It cost me some detail in various scenarios, like Quad9 becoming QuadN, and truncating long error lines, but it was worth the peace of mind.

In the end, the result was a list of up to eight bullets delivered to my ntfy instance each morning. One glance at it and I am good for the day.

A small job for an old laptop

The takeaway? I am keeping the model and script running on my home server for now. Not as is, but after tweaking the script based on what I find once it has run for a few more days. The five days of running already pointed me to a few issues, and another few days will gather more. But keeping it running also means I will have to keep in mind that even though it can get the container right, it can sometimes get details wrong too.

item.itunes:title: I gave Claude Code access to my Proxmox server, and it set up in 20 minutes what took me a weekend
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Back in September, getting trusted HTTPS certificates onto my home lab ate the best part of a weekend. I had Claude helping in a chat window the whole time, and I still spent hours copying commands into a terminal, pasting errors back, and fighting the DNS challenge that proves you own a domain when none of your services face the internet. It worked in the end, and Caddy replaced the reverse proxy config I dreaded.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

So I wondered what would happen if I cut myself out of the loop. Same job, new subdomain, but this time Claude Code would run the commands on my Proxmox server itself. It took 20 minutes. I also learned exactly how much of that I should take on trust.

I tried using a Proxmox-based Windows 11 VM as my daily driver - here's how it went

All it took was a little bit of tinkering and a whole lot of patience

12
By  Ayush Pande

I didn't exactly give Claude Code a lot to go on

An SSH key, two API tokens, and a short paragraph of instructions

"Access" sounds scarier than it was, although it was still plenty. Claude Code got root SSH to my Proxmox node, a Cloudflare API token that could edit DNS records on one domain and nothing else, and an API token for Technitium, which is still the best local DNS tool you can deploy. I've connected Claude to my Proxmox cluster through MCP before, but I left those servers out this time, so there was no special tooling involved, just a shell and two keys in a file.

The prompt named the outcome and left the method alone. I wanted three addresses under a new home. subdomain, for the Proxmox dashboard, the Technitium dashboard, and Jellyfin, to load in the browser on my PC with a trusted certificate and no warnings. Then I added three limits: nothing reachable from the internet, build it in a new container, and do not modify existing containers. That last sentence mattered more than anything else I typed.

I had to block its skills before the test meant anything

My first attempt lasted about a minute. Claude Code loaded a skill I'd written that maps my home lab, followed it to my lab notes, and started reading the note from September's build. That's smart behavior, and it's also the answer sheet.

To be fair, you could argue that's the point of keeping notes. But I wanted to know what access alone was worth, so I stopped the session and tried renaming my skills folder, which didn't work because the skills sync straight back from my account on launch. Starting the session with claude --disallowedTools "Skill" did the trick, and the permissions screen confirmed the block before I pasted the prompt again.

Your CLAUDE.md is probably wrong, and here's how Anthropic's engineers actually structure theirs

Your file is probably doing more harm than good

1
By  Mahnoor Faisal

Twenty minutes later, my Proxmox login had a padlock

And a new container, a wildcard certificate, and a working console

I sent the prompt at 11:17 pm. Claude Code's first report came back 14 minutes and 34 seconds later by its own timer, and at 11:37 pm I had "Connection is secure" on my Proxmox dashboard in Chrome, with a virtual machine's console running through the new address. Twenty minutes, start to padlock.

In that time it built a new container running nginx and certbot, got a wildcard certificate from Let's Encrypt using the DNS challenge through Cloudflare, created the DNS zone on my Technitium cluster, and put a firewall on the container that only accepts web traffic from my own network. My own check afterward agreed with its report: all three names resolved privately, had no public record, and served a certificate Windows trusts.

It skipped Caddy, and the hard parts of my weekend never showed up

Here's where I have to admit my test was designed around the wrong tool. I'd planned five traps based on September, and three of them only exist if you use Caddy. Its stock package doesn't include the Cloudflare DNS module, and its check that the challenge record has gone live gets tangled with how my eero mesh intercepts DNS.

Claude Code never met any of that, because it picked certbot instead. Its script created the record, waited 30 seconds, and let Let's Encrypt do the checking. The one trap that did apply was whether it would test against Let's Encrypt's staging servers before asking for a real certificate, and it did that without being told.

The problems it did hit weren't the ones I planned for

It still had a bumpy ride, just a short one. Its firewall rules didn't load the first time, and it noticed because it read the active ruleset back instead of assuming. The file holding the Cloudflare token came out five bytes longer than it expected, and its remote commands broke on PowerShell's quoting twice, so it moved the logic into script files on the server.

My favorite catch came after every check had already passed. The new container had picked up a public IPv6 address on its own, which it said would answer pings from the internet, and Claude Code went back and closed that off. I wouldn't have thought to look.

We've got IPv4 and IPv6, yet nobody really talks about IPv5

What was IPv5? You might be surprised to learn it never really existed.

5
By  Adam Conway

It never asked my permission, and my only input was a typo

Zero approval prompts, one blocked command

I didn't approve a single action during the run. The session was in auto mode, which is now Claude Code's default, with the stock rules, and a new container, a DNS zone, and a certificate all went through without a prompt. If that makes you a little uneasy, good, because it should.

Auto mode did block one command. Claude Code wanted to read the first and last few bytes of that Cloudflare token file to find the stray characters, and the block came back marked as unauthorized access. It didn't argue. It said it wouldn't inspect a secret file, then rewrote the file through a script that strips the junk on the way in.

The only line it wouldn't cross was the one I wrote

Jellyfin is the address that didn't fully work, and it wasn't Claude Code's fault. Without any hint from me, it turned out my Jellyfin container hasn't started since November 8 because its config passes through an AMD graphics device, and I've temporarily moved my Proxmox drives into an Intel box. The fix it proposed was to remove one line, which meant editing an existing container, so it stopped and asked.

And then I flubbed it. I typed a single "n" into the wrong window, meaning to log a note in my timer script, and Claude Code read it as "no" and left Jellyfin alone. So the one decision a human made in the whole run was a typo. Jellyfin's address still got its trusted certificate, with a polite error page behind it.

I set up Claude Code the way its creator does, and the difference is night and day

Who better to learn from than the person who made it?

19
By  Mahnoor Faisal

I'd hand Claude Code the keys again, with a tighter prompt

The September and November versions of this job both had Claude behind them. What changed was that I stopped being the slow, error-prone cable between the chat window and the terminal, and a weekend became 20 minutes. That time excludes my prep, which included discovering that my server didn't trust my SSH key yet.

What kept it safe wasn't a permission system, because nothing prompted me. It was a scoped token, a default that refused to peek at a secret, and "do not modify existing containers" in the prompt. Everything it built was additive, so tearing it down the same night took a few minutes, although its own rollback list left out the notes it had saved about my network on my PC. If you try this, write your limits down first, and ask for the evidence behind anything in the report you plan to rely on.
